defaultValue: Feel the time as a vibration pattern. Bind PulseTime to Quick Launch (hold Up or Down) for a one-gesture time check. Everything here can also be set on the watch without looking at it: Select repeats, Up/Down step through the seven rungs of the system cycle, holding Up/Down cycles the speed, and holding Select opens Practice. Each change answers with a short count of pulses before the time — short pulses count the rung, long pulses count the speed.

items.label: Time system
items.description: Terse Quarter: hour pulses, a pause, then quarter-hour pulses. Five-Minute Ladder: hours, five-minute steps, leftover minutes. Decimal Place: hours, minute tens, minute ones. Binary Clock: four hour bits then six minute bits (short = 0, long = 1). Nearest-Quarter Offset: nearest quarter, a before/after marker, then the offset in minutes. Morse Digits: the displayed digits as Morse numerals.

items.label: Playback speed
items.description: Slow stretches every pulse and pause by 25%; Fast shortens them by 22%.

items.label: Exact minutes (Terse Quarter only)
items.description: Adds short ticks for the leftover minutes inside the quarter. Only Terse Quarter needs this; the other five systems are inherently exact to the minute. On the watch this is rung 2 of the Up/Down cycle rather than a separate control.

items.defaultValue: Bind PulseTime to both Quick Launch buttons (Settings > Quick Launch on the watch) and each one can answer a different question. Holding Up can give you just the hour while holding Down gives just the minutes, so a glance-sized question takes a glance-sized pattern. Hours only and minutes only are not a new code to learn: each is exactly the half of your chosen time system you already know. If a half is empty — no five-minute steps at the top of the hour — you get one long pulse meaning none, because silence would just look broken. Once the app is open, any button press plays the whole time again.
Needs a watch that reports which button launched the app: Pebble Time 2, Pebble 2 Duo, or Pebble Round 2. On older Pebbles both settings are ignored and every launch plays the whole time.

The Pebble Time 2 and Pebble 2 Duo have a speaker, and PulseTime can play the same rhythm as notes. This is not decoration: several time systems separate hours from five-minute steps from leftover minutes by STRENGTH, and a Pebble motor has no strength control at all, so that dimension is simply lost when you feel it. On the speaker it comes back as pitch — stronger means higher — which is often easier to read than strength ever was. Sound is off by default, and the watch's own mute setting is always obeyed.
Needs a watch with a speaker: Pebble Time 2 or Pebble 2 Duo. On every other Pebble, including Pebble Round 2, these settings do nothing.

The time, with no gesture and nothing on screen beforehand. This is the one part of PulseTime that does not depend on what you are looking at: the watch launches PulseTime at the chosen moment, it buzzes, and it closes itself again. Nothing runs in between, so it costs no battery while it waits, and it does not take the watch's single background-worker slot. On the hour it strikes just the hour, the way a chiming clock always has; at a quarter or a half it plays the whole time, because there the minutes are the point.

Quiet hours silence chimes only — every deliberate way of asking still answers, including at three in the morning, which is exactly when you want the time without turning on a light. Set both to the same hour for no quiet period. Pebble allows an app only eight scheduled wake-ups at a time, so PulseTime books the next few and tops them up each time it runs; quarter-hourly therefore looks a couple of hours ahead and hourly most of a day. The watch screen shows how many are actually booked, because “chimes are on” and “a chime will really happen” are different claims.

items.label: Flick to tell time
items.description: Double-tap your wrist twice in the same direction, within about a second, from any watchface and PulseTime tells you the time. Read the costs first: a background worker has to run continuously, which uses battery all day. A Pebble can run only ONE background worker at a time, so turning this on may ask you to take the slot from another app, and another app can take it back. Pebble cannot vibrate from the background at all, so PulseTime briefly opens on screen to buzz and then closes itself and returns you to your watchface. If you would rather spend no battery, leave this off and bind PulseTime to Quick Launch instead: hold Up or Down from any watchface.

defaultValue: Pebble motors have no strength control, so every system here relies on pulse length and rhythm only. No PulseTime system depends on strength alone.
